``` ::: ::: ### Training portfolio averages by hand The structural audit above checks preparation across the source rows. Outcome summaries and exploration below use training policies only. The training portfolio averages are the exposure-weighted means of the rates. Because frequency, severity, and pure premium are each a risk-volume rate, the weighted mean of the rate equals the unweighted ratio of the underlying claim amounts: ::: {#c01c475b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} avg_frequency = splits.train["ClaimNb"].sum() / splits.train["Exposure"].sum() avg_frequency_check = np.average(splits.train["Frequency"], weights=splits.train["Exposure"]) avg_pure_premium = splits.train["ClaimAmountCapped"].sum() / splits.train["Exposure"].sum() avg_pure_premium_check = np.average(splits.train["PurePremium"], weights=splits.train["Exposure"]) print(f"Average frequency: {avg_frequency:.6f} claim / year") print(f" check (weighted mean of rate): {avg_frequency_check:.6f}") print(f"Average pure premium: {avg_pure_premium:.2f} EUR / year") print(f" check (weighted mean of rate): {avg_pure_premium_check:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Average frequency: 0.073705 claim / year check (weighted mean of rate): 0.073705 Average pure premium: 137.57 EUR / year check (weighted mean of rate): 137.57 ``` ::: ::: The two ways of writing the average are identical because each rate is defined as `amount / volume`. The same identity is what makes the target × weight multiplication collapse to the underlying claim amounts in `portfolio_calibration_table` and `evaluate_predictions`. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Look inside: `TARGET_SPECS` and `target_and_weight` `TARGET_SPECS` defines the targets and weights for frequency, severity, and pure premium. The `target_and_weight` helper returns the corresponding data. Step-by-step: 1. **Look up** the `TargetSpec` for the requested component in the `TARGET_SPECS` dict (frequency, severity, or pure_premium). 2. **Slice the rows** if `claims_only` is `True` (used for severity), keeping only policies with `ClaimNb > 0`. 3. **Return** `(rows, target_array, weight_array)`, the target array is the chosen column, the weight array is the row-appropriate exposure or claim count. ::: {#ec67475a .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} show_source(target_and_weight) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} ```python def target_and_weight( data: pd.DataFrame, component: str, ) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: """Return the rows, target, and weights for one pricing component.""" spec = TARGET_SPECS[component] rows = data.loc[data["ClaimNb"] > 0] if spec.claims_only else data return ( rows, rows[spec.target].to_numpy(dtype=float), rows[spec.weight].to_numpy(dtype=float), ) ``` ::: ::: - `frequency` uses target `Frequency` with weight `Exposure` over all policies. - `severity` uses target `Severity` with weight `ClaimNb` over **claims only**, the `claims_only` flag filters rows to `ClaimNb > 0` so the average is the claim-count-weighted mean of capped policy-average severity. - `pure_premium` uses target `PurePremium` with weight `Exposure` over all policies. Multiplying by exposure recovers the total capped claim amount. ::: ## Explore uncapped training outcomes before fitting These constant-mean references adapt the exploratory plots in the [GLUM motor tutorial](https://glum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/glm_french_motor_tutorial/glm_french_motor.html). Use every training policy, accounting for unequal exposures and claim counts. Severity here is uncapped; the capped modelling targets remain unchanged. Tail disagreement can expose limitations of a reference. Pooled agreement cannot establish conditional model validity or select a model family. Nothing here fits a model or predicts a policy: each reference uses a single constant portfolio mean, whereas section 3.7 repeats the comparison against the fitted model's policy-specific predictions. ### Frequency with unequal exposures The intercept-only annual rate is total claims divided by total exposure. Compare exposure-weighted count proportions with the same weighted mixture of Poisson distributions, each with mean $e_i\hat\lambda$. A Poisson at the annual rate alone would treat every policy as a full year. Keep zero claims and a final overflow bin, so both probability distributions sum to one. Exposure and risk mixing can inflate marginal count variance even under a valid conditional Poisson model, so assess dispersion around fitted policy means in the later area residual-dispersion table. ::: {#exploratory-frequency .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} exploration_train = splits.train exploration_exposure = exploration_train["Exposure"].to_numpy(dtype=float) exploration_counts = exploration_train["ClaimNb"].to_numpy(dtype=int) exploration_rate = exploration_counts.sum() / exploration_exposure.sum() count_max = int(exploration_counts.max()) count_bins = np.arange(count_max + 2) count_observed = np.bincount( exploration_counts, weights=exploration_exposure, minlength=count_max + 2 ) / exploration_exposure.sum() count_means = exploration_exposure * exploration_rate count_reference = np.array([ np.average(poisson.pmf(k, count_means), weights=exploration_exposure) for k in range(count_max + 1) ] + [np.average(poisson.sf(count_max, count_means), weights=exploration_exposure)]) print(f"All {len(exploration_train):,} training policies; Estimate $\hat\mu=\sum_i n_i y_i/\sum_i n_i$ and fit base dispersion with `fit_gamma_dispersion` at that constant mean. Each policy contributes once to its likelihood. Under independent Gamma claims with a common mean, $y_i$ has shape $n_i/\phi$ and scale $\phi\mu/n_i$. Both the empirical distribution and the Gamma reference use claim-count weights. ::: {#exploratory-severity-reference .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} uncapped_severity_rows = splits.train.loc[splits.train["ClaimNb"] > 0].copy() uncapped_severity_rows["UncappedSeverity"] = ( uncapped_severity_rows["ClaimAmountOriginal"] / uncapped_severity_rows["ClaimNb"] ) uncapped_y = uncapped_severity_rows["UncappedSeverity"].to_numpy(dtype=float) uncapped_n = uncapped_severity_rows["ClaimNb"].to_numpy(dtype=float) uncapped_mean = np.average(uncapped_y, weights=uncapped_n) uncapped_phi = fit_gamma_dispersion( uncapped_y, np.full_like(uncapped_y, uncapped_mean), uncapped_n ) mixture_counts, mixture_policies = np.unique(uncapped_n, return_counts=True) mixture_weights = mixture_counts * mixture_policies / uncapped_n.sum() severity_grid = np.geomspace(uncapped_y.min(), uncapped_y.max(), 512) severity_shape = mixture_counts / uncapped_phi severity_scale = uncapped_phi * uncapped_mean / mixture_counts severity_density = gamma.pdf( severity_grid[:, None], a=severity_shape, scale=severity_scale ) @ mixture_weights severity_survival = gamma.sf( severity_grid[:, None], a=severity_shape, scale=severity_scale ) @ mixture_weights severity_x, severity_empirical_sf = weighted_empirical_ccdf(uncapped_y, uncapped_n) print( f"All {len(uncapped_y):,} claim-bearing training policies; {int(uncapped_n.sum()):,} claims; " f"uncapped mean={uncapped_mean:,.2f} EUR; base phi={uncapped_phi:.6g}; " f"maximum policy average={uncapped_y.max():,.2f} EUR" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` All 19,955 claim-bearing training policies; 21,146 claims; uncapped mean=2,346.72 EUR; base phi=1.54079; maximum policy average=4,075,400.56 EUR ``` ::: ::: The histogram uses logarithmic amount bins with density per euro. This is not the ordinary weighted variance of policy averages. Retain groups with at least four claims and two claim-bearing policies. The table reports counts and exclusion reasons, including zero variance. ::: {#exploratory-severity-groups .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} severity_group_tables = {} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5)) for by, axis in zip(("VehPower", "BonusMalus"), axes): grouped = uncapped_severity_rows.groupby(by, observed=True) table = grouped.agg( policies=("ClaimNb", "size"), claims=("ClaimNb", "sum"), amount=("ClaimAmountOriginal", "sum"), ) table["mean"] = table["amount"] / table["claims"] policy_means = grouped["ClaimAmountOriginal"].transform("sum") / grouped["ClaimNb"].transform("sum") residual_squares = uncapped_severity_rows["ClaimNb"] * ( uncapped_severity_rows["UncappedSeverity"] - policy_means ) ** 2 table["V"] = residual_squares.groupby(uncapped_severity_rows[by], observed=True).sum() / ( table["policies"] - 1 ).replace(0, np.nan) table["status"] = "included" sparse = (table["claims"] < 4) | (table["policies"] < 2) table.loc[~sparse & (table["V"] == 0), "status"] = "zero variance: excluded from logs" table.loc[sparse, "status"] = "sparse: excluded" severity_group_tables[by] = table.drop(columns="amount") print_frame(f"Uncapped severity by {by} (all observed claim-bearing groups)", severity_group_tables[by]) print(f"{by}: {int(sparse.sum())} sparse groups; The Pearson estimate $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i e_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2/\hat\mu_i^p$ supplies only the starting value; a failed optimization raises. `tweedie_log_likelihood` uses [GLUM's scalar-dispersion density API](https://glum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/glm.html#glum.TweedieDistribution.log_likelihood) with $a_i=e_i^{1/(2-p)}$, transformed observations $a_i y_i$, transformed means $a_i\hat\mu_i$, and unit likelihood weights. It adds the Jacobian $\sum_{y_i>0}\log a_i$ for positive rates. Zero claims retain their probability mass, with no Jacobian term. Targets and weights follow the [GLUM motor tutorial](https://glum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/glm_french_motor_tutorial/glm_french_motor.html). ::: {#f9497820 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} show_source(select_tweedie_power) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} ```python def select_tweedie_power( development_train: pd.DataFrame, development_validation: pd.DataFrame, powers: tuple[float, ...] = TWEEDIE_POWERS, ) -> tuple[float, pd.DataFrame]: """Select p by validation profile likelihood under the fitted rate convention.""" train_rows, y_train, w_train = target_and_weight(development_train, "pure_premium") validation_rows, y_validation, w_validation = target_and_weight( development_validation, "pure_premium" ) results = [] for power in powers: family = TweedieDistribution(power) model = GeneralizedLinearRegressor( family=family, link="log", formula=RATING_FORMULA, drop_first=True, alpha=0, max_iter=200, ).fit(train_rows, y_train, sample_weight=w_train) train_prediction = model.predict(train_rows) validation_prediction = model.predict(validation_rows) dispersion = fit_tweedie_dispersion(y_train, train_prediction, w_train, power) log_likelihood = tweedie_log_likelihood( y_validation, validation_prediction, w_validation, power, dispersion ) results.append( { "power": power, "training_dispersion": dispersion, "validation_log_likelihood": log_likelihood, } ) profile = pd.DataFrame(results) if not np.isfinite(profile["validation_log_likelihood"]).all(): raise RuntimeError("Tweedie profile likelihood produced non-finite values") selected = float( profile.loc[profile["validation_log_likelihood"].idxmax(), "power"] ) return selected, profile ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Fit an interpretable GLUM benchmark An interpretable, stable benchmark tells us whether a flexible model earns its extra complexity. Fit a regularized GLUM for prediction, then a separate unregularized GLUM for coefficient relativities with sandwich standard errors. Confidence intervals from the unregularized model are not inference for the penalized predictive fit. Review relativities for plausibility, but choose predictions with out-of-sample evidence. `fit_glum_predictive` profiles 3-fold cross-validation over $\alpha \times \mathrm{l1\_ratio}$. For severity, it appends zero-weight anchor rows so categories absent in the training data still receive a defined prediction. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Look inside: `RATING_FORMULA` ``` C(VehBrand) + C(VehPower) + C(VehGas) + C(Region) + C(Area) + bs(VehAge, df=5, lower_bound=0, upper_bound=100) + bs(DrivAge, df=5, lower_bound=18, upper_bound=100) + bs(BonusMalus, knots=[55, 65, 80, 100], lower_bound=0, upper_bound=230) + LogDensity ``` ::: For the full implementation see [`src/nonlife_pureprem/pure_premium.py`](https://github.com/ThomasBury/nonlife-pureprem/blob/main/src/nonlife_pureprem/pure_premium.py) (`fit_glum_predictive`, `fit_glum_inference`). ::: {#f3284a05 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} glum_models = {} for component in TARGET_SPECS: glum_models[component] = fit_glum_predictive( splits.train, component, selected_power, n_alphas=n_alphas, ) inference = fit_glum_inference(splits.train, component, selected_power) relativities = coefficient_relativity_table(inference) print_frame(f"GLUM {component} relativities", relativities) print( f"GLUM {component}: alpha={glum_models[component].alpha_:.6g}, " f"l1_ratio={glum_models[component].l1_ratio_:.1f}" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

This section compares observations with predictions. The GLUM benchmark of the previous section supplies a policy-specific mean to every eligible training row of each component, and each reference below is the conditional distribution that prediction implies: a Poisson or Negative Binomial count with mean $e_i\hat\lambda_i$, a Gamma policy-average severity with mean $\hat\mu_i$, and a Tweedie capped policy total with mean $e_i\hat\mu_i$. The panels therefore compare observations with the predictions of the model fitted in section 3.6; the only quantities fitted below are dispersion parameters. These post-fit training diagnostics use capped targets and fitted policy means. The survival curves compare upper tails, the zero-mass table retains the two point masses, and the Pearson residual check compares conditional variation. All portfolio mixtures use the same risk-volume weights as their empirical counterparts; pooled agreement is not a formal assumption test or test-set performance evidence. | Observable | Conditional reference | Curve weight | | --- | --- | --- | | Policy claim count | Poisson mean $e_i\hat\lambda_i$ | Exposure $e_i$ | | Positive capped policy-average severity | Gamma shape $n_i/\phi$, scale $\phi\hat\mu_i/n_i$ | Claim count $n_i$ | | Capped policy total | Tweedie mean $e_i\hat\mu_i$, dispersion $\phi e_i^{1-p}$ | Exposure $e_i$ | ### Fit dispersion parameters; means stay fixed No mean is estimated here. Predicted rates stay fixed; the only fitted quantities are the Gamma base dispersion for severity, the Tweedie base dispersion for pure premium, and the Negative Binomial shape for frequency, each estimated on every eligible training row against the fixed predictions. The Gamma and Tweedie references thus share the model's policy means and working families with only a variance parameter estimated, and the Poisson count reference needs nothing fitted at all: its policy means come straight from the model. Only after those fits finish, sample up to 20,000 policies per component with seed 42 and reuse each component's rows, predictions, and weights throughout. ::: {#fit-diagnostic-parameters .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} training_rows = {} training_predictions = {} for component in TARGET_SPECS: rows, _, _ = target_and_weight(splits.train, component) training_rows[component] = rows training_predictions[component] = pd.Series( glum_models[component].predict(rows), index=rows.index, dtype=float ) severity_train = training_rows["severity"] gamma_dispersion = fit_gamma_dispersion( severity_train["Severity"], training_predictions["severity"], severity_train["ClaimNb"], ) nb_shape = fit_negative_binomial_shape( training_rows["frequency"]["ClaimNb"], training_rows["frequency"]["Exposure"] * training_predictions["frequency"], ) tweedie_dispersion = fit_tweedie_dispersion( training_rows["pure_premium"]["PurePremium"], training_predictions["pure_premium"], training_rows["pure_premium"]["Exposure"], selected_power, ) dispersions = {"frequency": 1.0, "severity": gamma_dispersion, "pure_premium": tweedie_dispersion} ``` ::: ::: {#cell-sample-diagnostic-policies .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} diagnostic_rows = {} diagnostic_predictions = {} for component, rows in training_rows.items(): sample = rows.sample(n=min(20_000, len(rows)), random_state=42) diagnostic_rows[component] = sample diagnostic_predictions[component] = training_predictions[component].loc[sample.index] print_frame( "Training diagnostic scope", pd.DataFrame({ "eligible_training_policies": {name: len(rows) for name, rows in training_rows.items()}, "plotted_policies": {name: len(rows) for name, rows in diagnostic_rows.items()}, "base_dispersion": dispersions, }), ) print(f"NB shape: {nb_shape:.6g} (infinity denotes the Poisson limit)") ``` ::: {#sample-diagnostic-policies .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
